findings.source_passage: moving his hand as with a hammer ... moving his hand as with a caulking-iron ... moving his hand as with a pitch-pot
findings.source_locator: Starbuck–Carpenter exchange, paragraphs after 'Rig it, carpenter'
findings.why_it_matters: The pantomime stage directions are a signature piece of Melville's theatrical voice and transform the exchange from dialogue into macabre performance; critics cite them as evidence of the book's dramatic-script register. Their removal flattens the scene into bare Q-and-A.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the parenthetical action tags ('moving his hand as with a hammer', etc.) for all three carpenter questions; they are short and load-bearing.

findings.source_passage: Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so—the coffin, I mean. Dost thou hear me? Rig it.
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's speech after the melancholy pause
findings.why_it_matters: The self-correction ('the coffin, I mean') and the repeated 'Rig it' are psychologically revealing; they show Starbuck's suppressed dread breaking through, a detail the critical tradition reads as his unwilling complicity in the voyage's doom. The draft's 'Rig it, carpenter' erases all of this.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full line verbatim: 'Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so—the coffin, I mean. Dost thou hear me? Rig it.'

findings.source_passage: It's the old woman's tricks to be giving cobbling jobs. Lord! what an affection all old women have for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who ran away with a bald-headed young tinker once.
findings.source_locator: Carpenter's soliloquy, after 'not a cobbler's job' passage
findings.why_it_matters: This digression is distinctively Melvillean—absurdist, comic, voice-establishing for the Carpenter as a character with an eccentric mental life. Its excision makes the monologue more workmanlike and less idiosyncratic, erasing a key note of the Carpenter's register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the old-woman-and-tinker anecdote and the Vineyard job-shop aside; these are short and functionally irreplaceable for the Carpenter's voice.

findings.source_passage: We work by the month, or by the job, or by the profit; not for us to ask the why and wherefore of our work, unless it be too confounded cobbling, and then we stash it if we can.
findings.source_locator: Carpenter's soliloquy, after 'bridal-bedsteads and card-tables' line
findings.why_it_matters: This line articulates the Carpenter's philosophy of unreflective labor—an important thematic counterweight to Ahab's obsessive purposiveness—and is part of the monologue's distinctive rhythmic and rhetorical texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this sentence in the Carpenter's soliloquy between the 'bridal-bedsteads' line and the 'thirty life-lines' passage.

summary: Four medium-severity losses: the carpenter's pantomime stage directions are entirely absent; Starbuck's psychologically charged self-correcting speech is flattened to a stub; the old-woman-tinker digression (voice-signature of the Carpenter) is cut; and the Carpenter's philosophy-of-labor line is missing—together these constitute significant voice erasure across the chapter's climactic exchange.
